description.para: The VCI method of Chen, Hillman and Rüter (2013) corrects the gradients of the test functions, $ \partial T_A / \partial Y_i = \partial N_A / \partial Y_i + \chi_A \sum_C \eta_{AiC}\, P_C $, such that the integration by parts is exact under the numerical integration for a polynomial basis $ P_C(Y) $ (the complete monomials up to the VCI order); $ \chi_A $ is the indicator of the support of kernel function $ A $, \[ \int_\Omega \frac{\partial T_A}{\partial Y_i} P_C \, dV + \int_\Omega T_A \frac{\partial P_C}{\partial Y_i} \, dV = \int_{\partial\Omega} T_A P_C n_i \, dA . \] The particles provide their local contributions to these integrals, all arrays are row-major, sized $ n_{\text{nodes}} \times n_{\text{dim}} \times n_C $ (index $ AiC $) or $ n_{\text{nodes}} \times n_C \times n_C $ (index $ ACD $), and contributions are accumulated (+=). The host framework assembles them over all particles per node $ A $ and solves $ \sum_D M_{ACD}\, \eta_{AiD} = R_{AiC} $ with the residual $ R_{AiC} = \int_{\partial\Omega} T_A P_C n_i\,dA - \int_\Omega \partial_i T_A\, P_C\,dV - \int_\Omega T_A\, \partial_i P_C\,dV $.

briefdescription.para: Get the number of VCI constraints $ n_C $ (the size of the polynomial basis).

Accumulate the moment matrix $ M_{ACD} = \int_\Omega \chi_A P_C P_D \, dV $ of the correction.
Assign the correction terms to the gradients of the test functions.

briefdescription.para: Describe the stiffness of the particle to a visitor, node by node: the shape functions at its evaluation point, then for every node the derivatives of its force with respect to the increment the particle interpolates (see StiffnessVisitor).

detaileddescription.para:
The stiffness is the tangent of computePhysicsKernels() at a zero increment, without the inertia: the material point is evaluated with the configuration of the last acceptStateAndPosition() and the working copy of the state. It is the stiffness of an accepted state after acceptStateAndPosition(), where an explicit host asks for it (in the middle of an increment, the working copy holds the advanced state, and the stiffness describes neither). Wherever it is called, the particle is left as it was found (state variables, and the response and the tangents the material point keeps). The default throws: a particle that does not describe its stiffness refuses a host that needs it, e.g. for the bound of the critical time step of an explicit scheme (addBoundOfAbsoluteStiffnessTimes() in MarmotParticleStiffnessVisitors.h).

briefdescription.para: The shape functions linearized about the center of the particle, $ G_B(\boldsymbol{Y}) = N_B(\boldsymbol{Y}_c) + \partial N_B / \partial \boldsymbol{Y} \cdot (\boldsymbol{Y} - \boldsymbol{Y}_c) $: the particle's own interpolation at its own points.

detaileddescription.para:
A particle knows every field it carries only by its value at its center, $ \sum_B N_B \boldsymbol{Q}_B $, and its (possibly smoothed) gradient there, $ \sum_B \boldsymbol{Q}_B \otimes \partial N_B / \partial \boldsymbol{Y} $, with the shape functions and gradients that drive its kinematics. At a point $ \boldsymbol{Y} $ of its own (its center, a vertex, a face center) its interpolation of a field is therefore the linearization about the center, \[ G_B = N_B(\boldsymbol{Y}_c) + \frac{\partial N_B}{\partial \boldsymbol{Y}} \cdot (\boldsymbol{Y} - \boldsymbol{Y}_c) , \] for every field: for the displacement, the motion of the point in the next increment, $ \Delta\boldsymbol{x} = \sum_B G_B\, \Delta\boldsymbol{Q}_B $ (the particle moves as a whole, its center with $ N_B $ and its domain with the homogeneous deformation gradient increment about the center); for a nonlocal field or a temperature, the value the particle carries at the point. It is not getInterpolationVector() at the point, $ N_B(\boldsymbol{Y}) $, except at the center: that one is exact at an arbitrary location, not the particle's view of its own points. A constraint that measures a field at a point of the particle and distributes its force with the same vector, $ \boldsymbol{f}_B = G_B\,\boldsymbol{f} $, has a symmetric stiffness and is conservative (the work of the force on the nodes is the work on the point). The vector sums to one (a rigid translation moves the point as the nodes). It has no default, unlike the methods next to it: the only candidate, the shape functions at the point, is not the particle's own interpolation.
vec
Array of $ n_{\text{nodes}} $ values.
coordinates
The point in the reference intermediate configuration (getDimension() values).

briefdescription.para: Evaluate the shape functions anew where the particle is now, with the kernel functions it holds.

detaileddescription.para: The shape functions of a particle are evaluated in its configuration (at its center, on its smoothing domain or on its subdomains): the trial functions $ N_A $, their (possibly smoothed) gradients $ \partial N_A / \partial Y_i $, and the test functions $ T_A = N_A $, which drops any VCI correction. acceptStateAndPosition() moves the particle, so they have to be evaluated anew in every increment. If the kernel functions that cover the particle changed, the host hands over the new ones with assignMeshfreeKernelFunctions(), which stores them and then calls this method. If they did not change, the host calls this method alone: the particle keeps its kernel functions, and with them its nodes and the layout of its residual and stiffness.

briefdescription.para: The section of the particle: what its integrals measure. A host that integrates other entities with the particles (finite elements, contact points on the faces of the particles) integrates them over the same measure: over the rings about the axis for Section::Axisymmetric, whose particles live in the meridian half plane $ (r, z) $.

simplesect.para: Section::Cartesian, unless a particle says otherwise.

briefdescription.para: Abstract interface of a particle of the reproducing kernel particle method (RKPM).

detaileddescription.para: A particle is the integration entity of the meshfree layer: it represents a piece of the body (its domain, commonly a point, a quadrilateral or a hexahedron) and it evaluates the weak form on that piece. Unlike a finite element, a particle has no fixed nodes. It interacts with the degrees of freedom, which live on the nodes of the meshfree kernel functions (KernelFunction), via the shape functions of a meshfree approximation (Approximation). The host framework (e.g., EdelweissMeshfree) finds the kernel functions whose support covers the particle and hands them over with assignMeshfreeKernelFunctions(); the particle then evaluates the shape functions $ N_A $ and (possibly smoothed) gradients $ \partial N_A / \partial Y $ of these $ A = 1 \dots n_{\text{nodes}} $ nodes.

Similar to finite elements, a particle computes the internal forces and their derivatives (computePhysicsKernels()), body loads (computeBodyLoad()) and distributed loads (computeDistributedLoad()). Concrete particles work in an updated Lagrangian setting: gradients are taken with respect to the coordinates $ Y $ of the last accepted (reference intermediate) configuration, and acceptStateAndPosition() moves the particle to the new configuration at the end of a converged increment.

A typical life cycle driven by the host framework is
creation via Marmot::Registry::ParticleFactory::createParticle(),
setProperties() (e.g., the order of the variationally consistent integration and time integration parameters),
assignStateVars() with a block of getNumberOfRequiredStateVars() doubles, initializeYourself(),
per increment: assignMeshfreeKernelFunctions(), or updateShapeFunctions() if the kernel functions that cover the particle did not change, optionally the VCI methods (vci_...), then repeatedly computePhysicsKernels() and the load methods, and after convergence acceptStateAndPosition().

That is an implicit increment. The calls of an explicit increment, in their order, and the three contracts that follow from it (a zero-length increment leaves the rates alone, an accept is idempotent, the material's tangent is required) are written down once, on the page "Meshfree Particles" of the documentation, section "The explicit life cycle of a particle". describeStiffness() is not one of them: it leaves the particle as it was found (and is of an accepted state after acceptStateAndPosition()).

State contract: the state variable block is a trial copy. Before every call of computePhysicsKernels(), the host restores it to the values committed by the last acceptStateAndPosition(), and dQ is the total increment since that state (not the Newton correction). Implementations may therefore update their state in place during computePhysicsKernels() (e.g. add the increment of the center displacement or of a nonlocal field to its committed value, or integrate velocities and accelerations), since every call starts again from the committed state; a cutback is simply a restore. EdelweissMeshfree implements this by copying the committed block into the trial block before each computePhysicsKernels() and back in acceptStateAndPosition().

For the residual vector and the stiffness matrix, unlike elements and cells, no (field-)blocked layout is possible. This is due to the fact that the number of nodes per particle is not fixed and may vary, and accordingly, the dofIndicesPermutationPattern used to designate the structure of a blocked storage may vary. Accordingly, for performance reasons, no dofIndicesPermutationPattern is provided, and the residual vector and the stiffness matrix are computed in a non-blocked, node-wise layout. Example: [node_1_displacement, node_1_temperature, node_2_displacement, node_2_temperature, ...], in which nodes designate the nodes of the kernel functions attached to the particle, in the order in which they were assigned. The size of both is thus $ n_{\text{nodes}} \cdot $ getNBaseDof().
For the stiffness matrix, a column-major layout is used.

The particle also offers the local contributions to the variationally consistent integration (VCI) of Chen, Hillman and Rüter (2013), see the vci_... methods. The global assembly and solution of the VCI correction is done by the host framework.

Methods added to this interface are appended at the end of the class, so that the vtable slots of the existing ones do not move: a library and a host built against different versions then fail on the one new call instead of silently calling the wrong method. This is why methods that belong together by subject may stand apart.
